title: Why the Sky Is Blue
summary: How sunlight is made of many colors, why tiny bits of air scatter blue light the most, and why sunsets, clouds, dusty days, and space look different.
poll: Anyone can explain why the sky is blue without being a scientist.

versions.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
versions.text:
Look up on a clear day. The sky is blue. But why?

Light from the sun looks white. But it is not just one color. It is a mix of all the colors. You can see them in a rainbow. There is red. There is green. There is blue.

Light moves in waves. Red light has long waves. Blue light has short waves.

The air has lots of tiny bits. They are much too small to see. When light hits them, it bounces off. It goes this way and that. We say the light scatters.

The bits scatter blue light much more than red. So blue light fills the sky. It comes at us from all sides. That is why the sky looks blue.

At sunset, the sun is low. Its light must pass through more air. Most of the blue is lost on the way. Red and gold light get through. So the sky glows red.

In space there is no air. So the sky there is black.

On a day with lots of dust, the sky looks pale or brown. Big bits of dust and sand scatter all the light.

versions.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
versions.text:
On a clear day, the sky is a bright blue. People have wondered why for a very long time. The answer has to do with light and air.

Light from the sun looks white. But white light is really a mix of all the colors. You can see them in a rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. A long time ago, Isaac Newton showed this. He shined sunlight through a piece of glass, and it split into colors.

Light travels in waves. Each color has a different size of wave. Red light has long waves. Blue and violet light have short waves.

The air around Earth is made of tiny bits of gas. They are much too small to see. When sunlight hits them, some of the light bounces off in all directions. Scientists say the light scatters.

These tiny bits scatter short waves much more than long waves. So blue light gets spread all over the sky. It reaches our eyes from every part of the sky, and the sky looks blue.

At sunset, the sun is low. Its light must travel through much more air to reach us. Most of the blue light is scattered away before it gets here. The red and orange light makes it through, so the sky glows red and gold.

In space there is no air. Nothing scatters the light, so the sky looks black. On a day with lots of dust, the sky can look pale or brown, because big bits of dust and sand scatter all the colors.

versions.title: The Science of a Blue Sky
versions.text:
On a clear day, the sky above us is a deep, bright blue. People have wondered about this color for thousands of years. The answer comes from the way sunlight and air work together.

Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of all the colors of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. In the 1660s, the English scientist Isaac Newton proved this. He passed sunlight through a glass prism, and the light spread out into a band of colors.

Light travels in waves. Each color has its own wavelength, which is the distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next. Red light has the longest wavelength we can see. Blue and violet light have much shorter wavelengths.

The atmosphere is the layer of air around Earth. It is made of tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. When sunlight hits these molecules, some of the light bounces off in many directions. Scientists call this scattering.

Gas molecules scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. So blue light gets spread across the whole sky. It reaches our eyes from every direction, and the sky looks blue. Violet light is scattered even more, but sunlight has less violet in it, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.

At sunset, the sun is low in the sky, so its light must pass through much more of the atmosphere. Most of the blue light is scattered away on the way. Mainly red and orange light reaches us, so the sky glows red and gold.

In space, there is no atmosphere to scatter light, so the sky looks black. On a dusty day, bigger bits of dust and sand scatter all the colors. Then the sky turns pale or brown.

versions.title: Scattered Light: Why the Sky Is Blue
versions.text:
On a clear afternoon, the sky above us shines a deep, brilliant blue, a sight so familiar that few people stop to question it. Curious thinkers wondered about this color for thousands of years, and the explanation depends on the way sunlight interacts with the invisible gases surrounding our planet.

Although sunlight appears white, it is actually a combination of all the colors of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. In the 1660s, the English scientist Isaac Newton demonstrated this by passing sunlight through a triangular glass prism. The light separated into a band of distinct colors, which proved that ordinary white light contains every one of them.

Light travels in waves, and each color has a particular wavelength, which is the distance from the peak of one wave to the peak of the next. Red light has the longest wavelength that human eyes can detect, while blue and violet light have considerably shorter wavelengths.

The atmosphere, the layer of air that surrounds Earth, consists of tiny gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, that are much smaller than a wavelength of light. When sunlight strikes these molecules, a portion of the light is redirected in many different directions, a process called scattering. In the 1870s, the British scientist Lord Rayleigh explained why such tiny particles scatter short wavelengths far more strongly than long ones, so this effect is now known as Rayleigh scattering.

Consequently, blue light is spread across the entire sky and reaches our eyes from every direction, which makes the sky appear blue. Violet light is scattered even more, but sunlight contains less violet, and human eyes are more sensitive to blue.

At sunset, the sun sits low on the horizon, so its light must travel through a much thicker section of the atmosphere before reaching us. Most of the blue light is scattered away during this long journey, and mainly red and orange light arrives at our eyes.

Clouds look white for a different reason. Their water droplets are much larger than gas molecules, so they scatter all colors about equally, and the mixed light appears white. In the same way, larger particles of dust and sand during a dust storm make the sky look pale or brownish. In space, where there is no atmosphere at all, nothing scatters the sunlight, so the sky looks completely black.

versions.title: Scattered Light: Why the Sky Is Blue
versions.text:
On a cloudless afternoon, the sky overhead glows a deep, brilliant blue, a sight so familiar that comparatively few people pause to interrogate its cause. Nevertheless, inquisitive thinkers speculated about this coloration for millennia, and the scientific explanation ultimately depends on the particular manner in which sunlight interacts with the invisible gases that envelop our planet.

Although sunlight appears uniformly white, it is in fact a composite of every color within the visible spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. During the 1660s, the English scientist Isaac Newton demonstrated this conclusively by directing a narrow beam of sunlight through a triangular glass prism, which separated the light into a continuous spectrum of distinct colors and established, beyond reasonable doubt, that ordinary white light contains every one of them simultaneously.

Light propagates in waves, and each color possesses a characteristic wavelength, defined as the distance separating the crest of one wave from the crest of the next. Red light possesses the longest wavelength that human eyes can perceive, whereas blue and violet light possess considerably shorter wavelengths.

The atmosphere, the protective envelope of air surrounding Earth, consists predominantly of nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are dramatically smaller than a wavelength of visible light. Whenever sunlight encounters these molecules, a proportion of it is redirected in numerous directions, a phenomenon known as scattering. During the 1870s, the British physicist Lord Rayleigh demonstrated mathematically why such minute particles scatter short wavelengths substantially more effectively than long ones, and this effect is consequently known as Rayleigh scattering.

As a direct result, blue light becomes distributed across the entire sky and reaches observers from every conceivable direction, which explains why the sky appears uniformly blue. Violet light is scattered even more intensely than blue, yet sunlight contains comparatively little violet to begin with, and human eyes are considerably more sensitive to blue than to violet; these two facts together explain why we perceive a blue sky rather than a violet one.

At sunset, sunlight must traverse a substantially thicker section of the atmosphere before reaching an observer, so most of the available blue light is scattered away during this extended journey, leaving predominantly red and orange illumination to reach our eyes directly, and this is why sunsets so often appear far more fiery than the sky at midday.

Clouds appear white for an entirely different reason: their water droplets are considerably larger than gas molecules, so they scatter all colors approximately equally, and this combined, undifferentiated illumination looks white rather than blue. Similarly, during a dust storm, comparatively large particles of dust and sand transform the sky into a pale or brownish haze, since these larger particles likewise scatter every wavelength about equally rather than favoring blue. In space, where no atmosphere exists whatsoever, nothing remains to scatter the sunlight, so the sky inevitably appears completely black, even in broad daylight.

In every one of these cases, then, it is ultimately the size of the particle doing the scattering, whether an invisible gas molecule, a visible water droplet, or a grain of windblown dust, that determines which colors reach our eyes and which sky we end up seeing.

versions.title: Scattered Light: Why the Sky Is Blue
versions.text:
On a cloudless afternoon, the sky overhead glows a deep, brilliant blue, a sight so thoroughly familiar that comparatively few people ever pause to interrogate its underlying cause. Nevertheless, inquisitive thinkers speculated about this particular coloration for millennia, and the scientific explanation ultimately depends on the precise manner in which sunlight interacts with the invisible gaseous envelope surrounding our planet.

Although sunlight appears uniformly white to the unaided eye, it is in fact a composite of every color within the visible spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. During the 1660s, the English scientist Isaac Newton demonstrated this conclusively by directing a narrow beam of sunlight through a triangular glass prism, which separated the light into a continuous spectrum of distinct, discernible colors and established, beyond reasonable doubt, that ordinary white light simultaneously contains every one of them.

Light propagates in waves, and each distinct color possesses a characteristic wavelength, defined precisely as the distance separating the crest of one wave from the crest of the subsequent wave. Red light possesses the longest wavelength that human eyes are capable of perceiving, whereas blue and violet light possess considerably, almost dramatically, shorter wavelengths by comparison.

The atmosphere, the protective gaseous envelope surrounding Earth, consists predominantly of nitrogen and oxygen molecules that are dramatically smaller than even a single wavelength of visible light. Whenever sunlight encounters these minuscule molecules, a proportion of it is redirected in numerous, essentially random directions, a phenomenon formally designated as scattering. During the 1870s, the British physicist Lord Rayleigh demonstrated mathematically, with considerable rigor, why such exceedingly minute particles scatter short wavelengths substantially more effectively than they scatter long ones, and this effect has consequently come to be known universally as Rayleigh scattering.

As a direct and unavoidable consequence, blue light becomes distributed uniformly across the entire sky and reaches observers from every conceivable direction simultaneously, which explains comprehensively why the sky appears uniformly blue rather than any other color. Violet light, admittedly, is scattered even more intensely than blue light, yet sunlight contains comparatively little violet radiation to begin with, and human eyes are considerably more sensitive to blue than to violet; these two interacting facts together explain conclusively why we perceive a blue sky rather than a violet one.

At sunset, sunlight must traverse a substantially thicker section of the atmosphere before ever reaching an observer's eyes, so the overwhelming majority of the available blue light is scattered away entirely during this extended journey, leaving predominantly red and orange illumination to arrive at our eyes directly and unimpeded.

Clouds appear white for an entirely different, unrelated reason: their constituent water droplets are considerably larger than ordinary gas molecules, so they scatter all colors of the spectrum approximately equally rather than favoring any single wavelength, and this combined, undifferentiated illumination consequently appears white rather than blue to an observer below. Similarly, during a dust storm, comparatively large particles of suspended dust and sand transform the sky into a pale or brownish haze, since these considerably larger particles likewise scatter every visible wavelength about equally rather than disproportionately favoring blue. In the vacuum of space, where no atmosphere exists whatsoever to intervene, nothing whatsoever remains to scatter incoming sunlight, so the sky inevitably appears completely and uniformly black, even during what would otherwise be broad daylight.

In every one of these distinct cases, then, it is ultimately the size of the particle performing the scattering, whether an invisible gas molecule, a visible water droplet suspended inside a cloud, or a coarse grain of windblown dust, that determines decisively which colors reach an observer's eyes and which particular sky that observer ends up seeing on any given day.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?

Why the sky looks blue and sometimes other colors
How to stay safe on a dusty day
Why the sun is hot

wrong.A: Rainbows are used to show that sunlight has many colors, but they are not the main topic.
wrong.C: Dust is only one small part, and the article gives no safety tips.
wrong.D: The article does not explain why the sun is hot.

wrong.B: Blue is only one of the colors in sunlight.

questions.stem: What did Isaac Newton show with a glass prism?

That the sky is black in space
That air is made mostly of nitrogen and oxygen gas
That red light has short waves

wrong.B: The article does not connect Newton to space.
wrong.C: The article does not say Newton studied the gases in air.
wrong.D: Red light has the longest wavelength, not short waves.

Nitrogen and oxygen

questions.stem: The article says human eyes are "more sensitive to blue." What does this mean?

Our eyes cannot see violet at all.
Our eyes notice blue more easily.
Blue light makes our eyes tired.
questions.why: Being sensitive to something means noticing or reacting to it easily, so our eyes pick up blue easily.

wrong.B: The article says sunlight has less violet, not that we cannot see it.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article mentions tired eyes.

questions.stem: Why is the sky not violet, even though violet light is scattered even more than blue?

Violet light has the longest wavelength.
Violet light is only made at sunset.
Sunlight has less violet, and our eyes notice blue more.

wrong.B: Violet has a short wavelength; red has the longest.

questions.stem: Why does sunlight lose more blue light at sunset than at noon?

Its path through the atmosphere is much longer.

wrong.A: The article explains the change by the light's trip through air, not by the sun changing.
wrong.C: The article does not say molecules change at night.

wrong.B: The air is still there; it just carries dust too.
wrong.C: The sun keeps shining during a dust storm.
wrong.D: The article calls dust particles larger, not smaller.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By telling a story about one scientist's life
By comparing two different planets
By giving facts step by step that lead to an explanation
By listing rules in order of importance
questions.why: The author explains white light, then wavelengths, then molecules and scattering, building step by step to why the sky is blue.

wrong.A: Newton is mentioned in only one paragraph.
wrong.B: The article does not compare two planets.
wrong.D: The article explains a science process; it does not list rules.

MID.prompt: Explain why the same sky can look blue at noon and red at sunset. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained both the blue sky and the red sunset.
I used at least two details from the article.
I used science words such as wavelength, scatter, or atmosphere correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: At noon, sunlight has a short path through the atmosphere, and the tiny gas molecules in the air scatter blue light, which has a short wavelength, far more than other colors, so the whole sky looks blue. At sunset the sun sits low on the horizon, so its light must travel through a much thicker layer of atmosphere before reaching us. Along that longer path, most of the blue light gets scattered away, leaving mainly red and orange light to color the sky.

keyWords.definition: the distance from the peak of one wave to the peak of the next
keyWords.example: Each musical note has its own wavelength of sound.

keyWords.definition: a very small drop of liquid

keyWords.definition: clearly separate and different from others
keyWords.example: The two birds have distinct songs, so it is easy to tell them apart.

questions.stem: Why do clouds look white, according to the article?

They absorb all of the red light.

wrong.B: Clouds are made of water droplets, not nitrogen molecules.
wrong.D: The article does not say clouds absorb red light.

Clearly separate from one another
Mixed together into white
Too faint to see

wrong.C: The prism did the opposite: it separated the mixed white light.

questions.stem: What is the effect of sunlight traveling through a thicker section of the atmosphere at sunset?
options: More violet light reaches our eyes.
The light stops being scattered at all once it gets near the ground.
Clouds turn black.
Most blue light is scattered away, leaving mainly red and orange.

wrong.B: A longer path causes more scattering, not none.
wrong.C: The article does not say clouds turn black at sunset.

questions.stem: Why does the size of a particle matter to the color of the sky?

Only particles larger than a wavelength can scatter light.

Particle size matters only in space.

wrong.A: Larger dust particles make the sky pale or brownish, not darker blue.

wrong.B: Blue light in sunlight must be scattered to fill the sky.

wrong.D: White clouds come from water droplets, which would not exist without an atmosphere.

To show how scientists built the explanation over time

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the size of particles in the air changes the color of the sky. Compare at least two examples from the article, such as a clear day, clouds, a dust storm, or space.
checklist: I clearly explained the link between particle size and sky color.
I compared at least two examples from the article.
I used precise words such as wavelength, scattering, and particle correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The size of the particles in the air determines which colors get scattered the most. On a clear day, tiny gas molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of light, so they favor scattering short blue wavelengths, which is why the sky looks blue. Clouds look completely different because their water droplets are much larger, so they scatter every distinct color of light about equally, producing a white color instead of blue. During a dust storm, the even larger dust particles also scatter all the colors evenly, which is why the sky turns a pale, brownish shade rather than its usual blue.
